claim: The factors determining the binding strength and search efficiency of eukaryotic TFs remain incompletely understood.

claim: Approximately 80% of TFs in eukaryotic cells have one or more intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs).
source: In eukaryotic cells, besides having a DNA-binding domain (DBD), approximately 80% of TFs also have one or more intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs), which lack a stable 3D structure and can be assumed as flexible, unstructured polymers, hundreds of amino acids (AAs) in length (Liu et al., 2006; Fuxreiter et al., 2011; Guo et al., 2011; Wright and Dyson, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Liu et al., 2006; Fuxreiter et al., 2011; Guo et al., 2011; Wright and Dyson, 2015.

claim: IDRs lack a stable 3D structure and can be assumed as flexible, unstructured polymers, hundreds of amino acids (AAs) in length.
source: In eukaryotic cells, besides having a DNA-binding domain (DBD), approximately 80% of TFs also have one or more intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs), which lack a stable 3D structure and can be assumed as flexible, unstructured polymers, hundreds of amino acids (AAs) in length (Liu et al., 2006; Fuxreiter et al., 2011; Guo et al., 2011; Wright and Dyson, 2015).

source: Eukaryotic DBDs often exhibit weaker affinity to their recognition sequences compared to their bacterial counterparts, indicating that IDRs are necessary for achieving stable binding (Garcia et al., 2021).

claim: IDRs are challenging to study because their functions can be maintained despite rapid sequence divergence.

source: Molecular dynamics simulations suggest that IDRs play a significant role in promoting target recognition (Vuzman and Levy, 2010), by increasing the area of effective interaction between the TF and the DNA.

claim: IDRs promote target recognition by increasing the area of effective interaction between the TF and the DNA.

claim: Truncation studies of IDRs in various TFs have demonstrated that removing these regions often results in reduced binding affinity.
source: Truncation studies of IDRs in various TFs have demonstrated that removing these regions often results in reduced binding affinity, suggesting they contribute significantly to stabilizing TF-DNA interactions (Brodsky et al., 2020).

claim: IDRs contribute significantly to stabilizing TF-DNA interactions.

claim: Some mechanisms propose non-specific electrostatic interactions to explain IDR contributions.
source: Different mechanisms have been proposed in the literature to explain IDR contributions: some suggest non-specific electrostatic interactions (Iwahara et al., 2006), others propose phase separation that concentrates TFs near their targets (Boija et al., 2018), while a third view suggests specific IDR-DNA interactions analogous to those of structured domains (Chappleboim et al., 2024).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Iwahara et al., 2006.

claim: Some mechanisms propose phase separation that concentrates TFs near their targets to explain IDR contributions.
source: Different mechanisms have been proposed in the literature to explain IDR contributions: some suggest non-specific electrostatic interactions (Iwahara et al., 2006), others propose phase separation that concentrates TFs near their targets (Boija et al., 2018), while a third view suggests specific IDR-DNA interactions analogous to those of structured domains (Chappleboim et al., 2024).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Boija et al., 2018.

claim: Some mechanisms propose specific IDR-DNA interactions analogous to those of structured domains to explain IDR contributions.

evidence: This is supported by citation to Chappleboim et al., 2024.

claim: Facilitated diffusion is a mechanism in which the TF performs 1D diffusion along the DNA and at any given moment can fall off and perform 3D diffusion until reattaching to the DNA.
source: One important mechanism is that of facilitated diffusion, in which the TF performs 1D diffusion along the DNA and at any given moment can fall off and perform 3D diffusion until reattaching to the DNA (a 3D excursion).
evidence: This is established knowledge about facilitated diffusion mechanism.

claim: The facilitated diffusion mechanism is well characterized theoretically.
source: This mechanism is well characterized theoretically (Berg et al., 1981; Berg and von Hippel, 1987; Slutsky and Mirny, 2004; Mirny et al., 2009; Li et al., 2009; Bénichou et al., 2011; Sheinman et al., 2012) and supported by experiments in E. coli (Hammar et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to theoretical work.

claim: The facilitated diffusion mechanism is supported by experiments in E. coli.
source: This mechanism is well characterized theoretically (Berg et al., 1981; Berg and von Hippel, 1987; Slutsky and Mirny, 2004; Mirny et al., 2009; Li et al., 2009; Bénichou et al., 2011; Sheinman et al., 2012) and supported by experiments in E. coli (Hammar et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Hammar et al., 2012.

claim: Due to significant structural differences, including larger genome size and chromatin structure, the facilitated diffusion mechanism cannot explain the fast search times observed in eukaryotes.
source: However, due to the significant structural differences, including larger genome size and chromatin structure, the facilitated diffusion mechanism cannot explain the fast search times observed in eukaryotes, and a qualitatively different mechanism is required (Dror et al., 2016; Jana et al., 2021; Ferrie et al., 2022; Kumar et al., 2023; Wagh et al., 2023).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Dror et al., 2016; Jana et al., 2021; Ferrie et al., 2022; Kumar et al., 2023; Wagh et al., 2023.

claim: A qualitatively different mechanism is required to explain TF search in eukaryotes.
source: However, due to the significant structural differences, including larger genome size and chromatin structure, the facilitated diffusion mechanism cannot explain the fast search times observed in eukaryotes, and a qualitatively different mechanism is required (Dror et al., 2016; Jana et al., 2021; Ferrie et al., 2022; Kumar et al., 2023; Wagh et al., 2023).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Dror et al., 2016; Jana et al., 2021; Ferrie et al., 2022; Kumar et al., 2023; Wagh et al., 2023.

claim: The binding of IDR to the DNA is energetically favorable.
source: The problem of binding affinity (binding probability) exhibits the classical trade-off between energy and entropy: on one hand, the binding of IDR to the DNA is energetically favorable.
evidence: This is based on fundamental thermodynamic principles.

claim: Binding of IDR to DNA leads to constraints on the positions of the IDR, which leads to a reduction in the entropy associated with the possible polymer conformations.
source: On the other hand, this binding leads to constraints on the positions of the IDR (pinned to the DNA at the points of attachment), which leads to a reduction in the entropy associated with the possible polymer conformations – hence an increase in the free energy of the system.
evidence: This is based on fundamental thermodynamic principles of entropy.

claim: The effects of the disordered tail on affinity are non-trivial, leading to physical problems reminiscent of those associated with the well-studied problem of DNA unzipping.
source: Therefore, the effects of the disordered tail on affinity are non-trivial, leading to physical problems reminiscent of those associated with the well-studied problem of DNA unzipping (Danilowicz et al., 2004).
evidence: This is an inference based on analogy to DNA unzipping, with citation to Danilowicz et al., 2004.

claim: The binding probability increases dramatically for TFs having IDRs for a broad parameter regime.
source: We find that the binding probability increases dramatically for TFs having IDRs for a broad parameter regime.
evidence: This is supported by the data and analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: The optimal search process consists of one round of 3D-1D search, where at first the TF performs 3D diffusion and then binds the antenna and performs 1D diffusion until finding its target, rarely unbinding for another 3D excursion.
source: The optimal search process consists of one round of 3D-1D search, where at first the TF performs 3D diffusion and then binds the antenna and performs 1D diffusion until finding its target, rarely unbinding for another 3D excursion.
evidence: This is supported by the data and analysis presented in the manuscript.

source: This process is presented in Figure 1a and c.

source: The experiment described in Brodsky et al., 2020 studied the binding affinity of wild-type and mutated TFs to their corresponding targets.

source: They found that shortening the IDR length results in weaker affinity.

source: Since the IDR is thought to recognize a relatively short flanking DNA sequence of the DBD target (Brodsky et al., 2020), we model a DNA segment as a straight-line 'antenna' region (Shimamoto, 1999; Hu and Shklovskii, 2007; Mirny et al., 2009; Castellanos et al., 2020), where the IDR targets reside.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Brodsky et al., 2020.

claim: The interaction between TF and DNA outside the antenna region is negligible.
source: We assume that the interaction between TF and DNA outside the antenna region is negligible.

source: Note that the interaction between IDR and DNA is a specific interaction, with genomic localization determined by multivalent interactions mediated by hydrophobic residues (Jonas et al., 2023; Mindel et al., 2024).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Jonas et al., 2023 and Mindel et al., 2024.

source: As we shall see, this design principle is also intact when multiple IDR sites and targets are involved, which is the scenario we discuss next.

source: Equation 4 is a direct consequence of the energy-entropy trade-off.

source: It means that the optimal search process is a single round of 3D diffusion followed by 1D diffusion along the antenna.

source: In Appendix 8, a single round of 3D-1D search is typically the case in the optimal search process., by analytically calculating the mean total search time using a coarse-grained model, we find that a single round of 3D-1D search is typically the case in the optimal search process.

claim: The model differs profoundly from the conventional facilitated diffusion (FD) model in bacteria.
source: Note that our model differs profoundly from the conventional facilitated diffusion (FD) model in bacteria: In the latter, the TF is assumed to bind non-specifically to the DNA.
evidence: This is a comparison between the current model and established models.

claim: The FD model requires numerous rounds of DNA binding-unbinding to achieve minimal search time.
source: As opposed to the FD model, which requires numerous rounds of DNA binding-unbinding to achieve minimal search time, within our model, the minimal search time is achieved for a single round of 3D and 1D search.
evidence: This is a comparison between the current model and the FD model.

claim: Within the model, the minimal search time is achieved for a single round of 3D and 1D search.
source: As opposed to the FD model, which requires numerous rounds of DNA binding-unbinding to achieve minimal search time, within our model, the minimal search time is achieved for a single round of 3D and 1D search.

claim: When observing the motion of a TF along the antenna, IDR sites behave like 'tentacles', constantly binding and unbinding from the DNA.
source: Interestingly, when we observe the motion of a TF along the antenna, IDR sites behave like 'tentacles', as illustrated in Figure 1c, constantly binding and unbinding from the DNA.
evidence: This is observed from the simulations and illustrated in Figure 1c.

claim: The 1D walk is referred to as 'octopusing', inspired by the famous 'reptation' motion in entangled polymers suggested by de Gennes.
source: We refer to this 1D walk as 'octopusing', inspired by the famous 'reptation' motion in entangled polymers suggested by de Gennes (de Gennes and Leger, 1982; see Video 1).
evidence: This is a naming convention inspired by work from de Gennes and Leger, 1982.

claim: Previous numerical studies used comprehensive, coarse-grained, MD simulations to demonstrate that including heterogeneously distributed binding sites on the IDR could facilitate intersegmental transfer between different regions of the DNA.
source: We note that previous numerical studies Vuzman and Levy, 2010; Vuzman and Levy, 2012 used comprehensive, coarse-grained, MD simulations to demonstrate that including heterogeneously distributed binding sites on the IDR could facilitate intersegmental transfer between different regions of the DNA, which is reminiscent of our octopusing scenario.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Vuzman and Levy, 2010 and Vuzman and Levy, 2012.

claim: Making the targets denser would hardly accelerate the search time, reminiscent of the well-known chemoreception problem where high efficiency is achieved even with low receptor coverage.
source: Making the targets denser would hardly accelerate the search time, reminiscent of the well-known chemoreception problem where high efficiency is achieved even with low receptor coverage (Berg and Purcell, 1977).
evidence: This is an analogy to the chemoreception problem, with citation to Berg and Purcell, 1977.

claim: For the 1D search from a single particle picture, since the TF is unlikely to detach once it attaches, it performs a 1D random walk.
source: For the 1D search from a single particle picture, since the TF is unlikely to detach once it attaches, it performs a 1D random walk.
evidence: This is an inference from the simulation results.

claim: Reducing the DNA persistence length, which promotes increased DNA coiling, results in only a modest increase in mean search time.
source: We have verified that reducing the DNA persistence length, which promotes increased DNA coiling, results in only a modest increase in mean search time.
evidence: This is verified by additional simulations shown in Appendix 9.

claim: Even under extreme coiling conditions, the increase in search time remains below 30% of the baseline value.
source: Even under extreme coiling conditions, the increase remains below 30% of the baseline value, as detailed in Appendix 9. Robustness of mean total search time with changing the antenna geometry.
evidence: This is supported by analysis shown in Appendix 9.

claim: The 3D diffusion coefficient slightly changes under a complex DNA configuration, where a point-searcher TF non-specifically interacts with the entire DNA, indicating the robustness of the optimal search process.
source: We also verified that the 3D diffusion coefficient slightly changes under a complex DNA configuration, where a point-searcher TF non-specifically interacts with the entire DNA, indicating the robustness of our optimal search process (see Appendix 10. MSD in a complex DNA configuration).
evidence: This is verified by additional simulations shown in Appendix 10.

claim: During the octopusing process, different IDR binding sites constantly bind and unbind from the antenna, leading to an effective 1D diffusion.
source: Next, we characterize the dynamics of the octopusing walk (Appendix 11. Properties of the octopusing walk). During this process, different IDR binding sites constantly bind and unbind from the antenna, leading to an effective 1D diffusion.
evidence: This is characterized in Appendix 11.

claim: Within the context of TF search in bacteria, the speed-stability paradox is known.
source: Indeed, within the context of TF search in bacteria, this is known as the speed-stability paradox (Slutsky and Mirny, 2004).
evidence: This is cited from Slutsky and Mirny, 2004.

claim: The simple picture of the octopusing walk explains an elegant mechanism to bypass the speed-stability paradox, achieving a high diffusion coefficient with a low rate of detaching from the DNA.
source: Importantly, the simple picture of the octopusing walk explains an elegant mechanism to bypass this paradox, achieving a high diffusion coefficient with a low rate of detaching from the DNA.
evidence: This is inferred from the analysis of the octopusing mechanism.

claim: The octopusing mechanism comes about due to the compensatory nature of the dynamics: there is, in effect, a feedback mechanism whereby if only a few sites are bound to the DNA, the on-rate increases, and similarly, if too many are bound the off-rate increases.
source: This comes about due to the compensatory nature of the dynamics: there is, in effect, a feedback mechanism whereby if only a few sites are bound to the DNA, the on-rate increases, and similarly, if too many are bound (thus prohibiting the 1D diffusion) the off-rate increases.
evidence: This is inferred from the analysis of the dynamics.

claim: The octopusing mechanism remains highly effective even when the typical number of binding sites is as low as two.
source: Remarkably, this mechanism remains highly effective even when the typical number of binding sites is as low as two.
evidence: This is supported by analysis shown in Appendix 11.

claim: In Brodsky et al., 2020, the binding probability of the TF Msn2 in yeast was measured, where the native IDR was shortened by truncating an increasingly large portion of it.
source: In Brodsky et al., 2020, the binding probability of the TF Msn2 in yeast was measured, where the native IDR was shortened by truncating an increasingly large portion of it.

source: The results indicate that binding probability decreases with increasing truncation of the IDR, as illustrated in Figure 4a.
evidence: This is from Brodsky et al., 2020 and shown in Figure 4a.

claim: The magnitudes and variations of k_on and k_off could be directly compared to experimental results in future studies.
source: The magnitudes and variations of these rates could be directly compared to experimental results in future studies.
evidence: This is a proposal for future experimental validation.

claim: The simplified model provides general design principles for the search process and testable predictions.
source: In summary, we addressed the design principles of TFs containing IDRs, with respect to binding affinity and search time. We find that both characteristics are significantly enhanced compared to simple TFs lacking IDRs. The simplified model we presented provides general design principles for the search process and testable predictions.
evidence: This is a summary of the work's contributions.

claim: One key assumption is that there exists a region on the DNA, close to the DBD target, that contains targets for the IDR binding sites.
source: One possible experiment that could shed light on one of our key assumptions is 'scrambling' the DNA (randomizing the order of nucleotides). Our results depend greatly on our assumption that there exists a region on the DNA, close to the DBD target, that contains targets for the IDR binding sites.
evidence: This is an explicit statement of a key assumption in the model.

claim: Shuffling a region smaller in length than the IDR should have minimal effect on the binding affinity and search time.
source: According to our results, we would expect that shuffling a region smaller in length than the IDR should have minimal effect on the binding affinity and search time, but that shuffling a region longer than the IDR should have a noticeable effect.
evidence: This is a prediction from the model for experimental testing.

claim: Shuffling a region longer than the IDR should have a noticeable effect on binding affinity and search time.
source: According to our results, we would expect that shuffling a region smaller in length than the IDR should have minimal effect on the binding affinity and search time, but that shuffling a region longer than the IDR should have a noticeable effect.
evidence: This is a prediction from the model for experimental testing.

claim: At short waiting times (within several seconds), the binding probability is expected to increase with waiting times.
source: At short waiting times (within several seconds), we would expect the binding probability to increase with waiting times.
evidence: This is a prediction from the model.

claim: The presence of the IDR in a TF leads to increased binding probabilities over various waiting times and a reduced waiting time to reach a higher saturation binding probability.
source: Our results suggest that the presence of the IDR in a TF leads to increased binding probabilities over various waiting times and a reduced waiting time to reach a higher saturation binding probability.
evidence: This is a prediction from the model.

claim: Higher-resolution molecular dynamics simulations could provide more detailed molecular insights and further validate the proposed design principles.
source: While our work primarily focused on coarse-grained modeling of the search process and the hypothesized octopusing dynamics, higher-resolution molecular dynamics simulations could provide more detailed molecular insights and further validate our proposed design principles (Vuzman and Levy, 2010; Vuzman and Levy, 2012).
evidence: This is a suggestion for future work with citations to relevant prior work.

claim: The design principles are grounded in fundamental physical concepts, such as the energy-entropy trade-off, and are likely to be robust across diverse molecular systems.
source: Since these principles are grounded in fundamental physical concepts, such as the energy-entropy trade-off, they are likely to be robust across diverse molecular systems.
evidence: This is an inference based on the fundamental nature of the principles.

claim: The design principles are anticipated to be applicable to other biophysical contexts, such as nonspecific RNA polymerase binding and multivalent antibody binding.
source: We anticipate their applicability to other biophysical contexts, such as nonspecific RNA polymerase binding (Tenenbaum et al., 2023) and multivalent antibody binding (Einav et al., 2019), where the associated dynamic processes would also be of significant interest for future research.
evidence: This is speculation about broader applicability with citations to related work.

claim: IDRs could facilitate complex formation and cooperativity between multiple transcription factors.
source: Beyond our octopusing mechanism, other mechanisms may also contribute to the search and binding process. IDRs could facilitate complex formation and cooperativity between multiple transcription factors, as suggested by studies showing co-localization at common target promoters (Morgunova and Taipale, 2017).
evidence: This is cited from Morgunova and Taipale, 2017.

claim: IDRs might enhance efficiency by directing transcription factors to specific nuclear compartments or biomolecular condensates, thereby reducing the effective search space and time.
source: IDRs might also enhance efficiency by directing transcription factors to specific nuclear compartments or biomolecular condensates, thereby reducing the effective search space and time (Sabari et al., 2018; Boija et al., 2018; Kent et al., 2020).
evidence: This is cited from Sabari et al., 2018; Boija et al., 2018; Kent et al., 2020.

claim: The findings represent one component of a broader regulatory framework governing transcriptional control in eukaryotic cells.
source: These complementary mechanisms (Ferrie et al., 2022; Jonas et al., 2025; Holehouse and Kragelund, 2024) suggest that our findings represent one component of a broader regulatory framework governing transcriptional control in eukaryotic cells.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the work's place in the broader context, with citations.

claim: The TF is coarse-grained by representing it with a few binding sites for the IDR, and an additional site for the DBD.

claim: The targets are assumed to be positioned at equal spacing, with one target for the DBD and a few targets for the IDR.
source: The targets are assumed to be positioned at equal spacing, with one target for the DBD and a few targets for the IDR, corresponding to the orange and black squares in Figure 1c.
evidence: This is an assumption in the model, illustrated in Figure 1c.

claim: Relaxing the assumption of equally spaced targets and using randomly positioned targets does not affect the results.
source: We have also verified that relaxing this assumption, and using randomly positioned targets, does not affect our results (Appendix 6. Robustness of the binding design principles).
evidence: This is verified by additional analysis shown in Appendix 6.

claim: The resulting search time is insensitive to the value of the threshold for treating the TF as a rigid body.
source: We verified that the resulting search time is insensitive to the value of this threshold.
evidence: This is verified by testing different threshold values.

claim: Due to the IDR trapped in the binding targets on the antenna, which results in slow dynamics, the simulation time becomes significantly longer.
source: Due to the IDR trapped in the binding targets on the antenna, which results in slow dynamics, the simulation time becomes significantly longer, as found in previous simulation studies (Vuzman and Levy, 2010; Marcovitz and Levy, 2013).
evidence: This is observed in the simulations and cited from previous work.

claim: The slowdown in simulation dynamics is similar to the behavior observed in glass-forming liquids.
source: This slowdown is similar to the behavior observed in glass-forming liquids (Berthier and Biroli, 2011).
evidence: This is an analogy to glass-forming liquids, with citation to Berthier and Biroli, 2011.
